The *spectral ordinate* $S_a(T_n)$ is the maximum acceleration reported by a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) oscillator with fundamental period $T_n$ and represents the seismic ground-motion defined of a given target service level for each structural period. The *response spectra* represent spectral ordinates $S_a(T_n)$ expressed in terms of the SDOF's fundamental period $T_n$ for a given target annual exceedance probability (AEP). The *uniform hazard spectra (UHS)* represents spectral ordinates $S_a(T_n)$ with the same probability of exceedance defined for all structural periods $T_n$. 


The design earthquakes for the project site are defined in terms of the site's response spectrum. Spectral ordinates defined at the structural period $T_n=0$ sec, are the *peak ground accelerations* $(pga)$. The $pga$ is the maximum acceleration experienced by a particle at the ground surface during an earthquake It represents the spectral acceleration, Sa(Tn), at a natural period of $T_n=0$ seconds, corresponding to an infinitely stiff system. $pga$  is a key parameter in seismic hazard assessment, often used as a primary indicator of earthquake intensity and for designing structures to withstand seismic forces. The *peak ground velocity* $(pgv)$ is an intensity measure, often derived from empirical models based on $pga$  and Arias Intensity is a strongly correlated measure with seismic demand in terms of permanent slope displacements and both are frequently used as a proxy for selecting seismic records for dynamic deformation analysis.


The  $pgv$ can be obtained from empirical (regression) models [^X2] based on peak ground accelerations. @Seed82 provided an estimate of median $(pgv)$ values (no error term reported) assuming a linear relationship as $pgv\approx (55 \ cm/s) \ pga/g$. A similar expression incorporating random uncertainty from a large dataset of seismic records can be obtained from the expression @eq-PGVR where $pgv$ is the median peak-ground velocity expressed in $m/s$, $pga^o$ are the peak-ground accelerations in rock expressed in units of $g$, and $\phi_1$ , $\phi_2$ are model parameters  [@Verri2023a].

$$pgv^o \approx \eta_{PGV}(pga^o) \approx  \phi_1 \ (pga^o/g)^{\phi_2} \  [m/s]$${#eq-PGVR}

 
The *Arias intensity* is an IM strongly correlated with seismic demand in terms of permanent settlement of slopes and are often used as a proxy for the selection of seismic records for dynamic deformation analysis.  In similar way as $pgv$, Arias Intensities ($ai$) can be obtained from a probabilistic model based on peak ground accelerations from @eq-AIR, where $ai$ is the median Arias Intensity in $m/s$, $pga$ are the peak-ground accelerations for rock site conditions in units of $g$ , $\psi_1$ , $\psi_2$ are model parameters
$$ai(pga^o) \approx  \eta_{A}(pga^o) \approx  \psi_1 \ (pga^o/g)^{\psi_2} \  [m/s]$${#eq-AIR}
